Use the same unit throughout: sets, pieces or another unit you define. Count only stock suitable for the intended teaching use. For reusable items, required quantity should reflect simultaneous demand; for consumables, include the entire planned usage. Quantity matching does not establish product suitability.

Avoided spend vs buying all new

This item plan is separate from the semester budget. Transfer its cost once to the appropriate budget category.

The purchasing decision

Supplier quotes may include minimum orders, discounts, tax and freight that are not modeled here. Avoided spend is a comparison at the same pack price, not a verified saving. Existing stock has not been inspected.

Why pack sizes change the decision

Shortfall = max(0, required − usable stock). Packs = shortfall ÷ pack size, rounded up. Leftover units = stock + purchased units − required. The all-new comparison rounds the full required quantity to whole packs at the same price. Existing stock may reduce the shortage without reducing the number of packs; in that case avoided spend is zero.

THE SEMESTER PLANNER

A clearer budget.
Before the purchase order.

Use your own supplier quotes and staffing estimates. The starting numbers are illustrative, not product prices or recommended lab requirements. All calculations stay in your browser.

Count each cost once. Include applicable tax, waste disposal, calibration and licenses in “other costs.” Use all sections' shared costs in the shared-supplies field. Staffing cost may already sit outside your purchasing budget.

ESTIMATED SEMESTER RESOURCE COST
Enrolled students
Cost per student
Purchases, before contingency
Staffing, before contingency
Contingency allowance

Planning estimate; no supplier pricing is implied.

How the calculation works

Students = students per section × sections. Purchases = students × consumables per student + new equipment + shared supplies + other costs. Staffing = sections × preparation hours × hourly staff cost. Total = (purchases + staffing) × (1 + contingency ÷ 100). Existing equipment is not re-purchased or depreciated in this model. Contingency applies to both purchases and staffing.

THE PRINCIPLE

A good teaching resource
starts with the course.

Learning comes first

ASM updated its undergraduate curriculum guidance in 2024. Use the learning goals, your syllabus and instructor judgment to define requirements before comparing products. Read the curriculum guidance ↗

Context matters

Teaching-lab resources need to fit the facilities, supervision and institutional requirements. ASM also publishes teaching-lab biosafety guidance. A product description or budget calculator cannot replace that review. Read the teaching-lab guidance ↗

BUILD · LEARN · IMPROVE

One small pilot.
One real buying decision.

Our working hypothesis: college microbiology lab coordinators need a clearer way to combine semester costs and purchasing requirements. We have not yet validated it with interviews.

THIS ITERATION

Make the decision visible

A stock-aware item planner, semester budget, exportable checklist and short supplier research list. No account or data collection needed.

NEXT VALIDATION

Work with six coordinators

Observe a recent or upcoming purchase. Test whether three can use the tools with real figures and name a concrete improvement.

THEN PRIORITIZE

Build what the pilot needs

Possible next steps: side-by-side quotes, equipment inventory or course-specific planning. Select one based on observed use.

Pilot targets are proposed project decisions, not industry benchmarks. No interviews or supplier applications have been completed.

RESEARCH & TRANSPARENCY

The evidence behind the pilot.

Carolina already offers buying guides and quote requests; Quartzy and LabArchives already support inventory and ordering. Our narrower hypothesis is connecting course requirements, class size and existing resources to a usable semester purchasing brief. Novelty and demand remain unproven.
